claims.text: Layer-by-layer in-situ deep cryogenic treatment during laser powder bed fusion will refine the microstructure of high-entropy alloys.
Layer-by-layer in-situ deep cryogenic treatment will relieve thermal and residual stresses.
Layer-by-layer in-situ deep cryogenic treatment will improve dimensional precision relative to conventional L-PBF.
Layer-by-layer in-situ deep cryogenic treatment will enhance mechanical integrity relative to conventional L-PBF.
Layer-by-layer in-situ deep cryogenic treatment will reduce fabrication-induced defects relative to conventional L-PBF.
Laser-additively manufactured high-entropy alloys accumulate thermal stress in the as-deposited state.
Rapid solidification in L-PBF causes significant residual stress, thermal distortion, and defect formation.
The proposed intervention is to apply DCT immediately after deposition of every layer.
The intervention will produce reduced residual stress and stabilized solidification fronts.
The rapid quenching from DCT will reduce thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients will lower residual stresses.
Rapid cryogenic cooling will stabilize the solidification interface.
A stabilized solidification interface will suppress defect nucleation and growth and reduce thermal distortion.
Post-process DCT has previously increased both tensile strength and elongation in a laser-deposited Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloy.
The expected benefits should extend to high-entropy alloys with thermal and microstructural behavior similar to the previously studied alloy.
The benefits are expected under typical L-PBF energy inputs and may not persist under extreme process parameters or alloy compositions.

Failure to obtain at least a 10% dimensional-accuracy improvement, measurable mechanical-property enhancement, and reduced defect density relative to an untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Rapid solidification is identified as a cause of residual stress and distortion, while an additional abrupt rapid-cooling step is asserted to reduce thermal gradients and stress without explaining why the added quench would have the opposite effect.
